Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO with government input
article:
Nvidia Corp.’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer, less than two weeks after his remarkable ouster, after US government intervention. Nvidia shares gained more than 31%.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, board chair, in a company statement Monday.

Huang’s return is effective immediately, according to the statement. The board reinstated Huang after a series of meetings and discussions and after receiving input from “senior levels of the United States government,” according to the company. “Based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

Huang, 63, oversaw Nvidia for more than three decades and built it into the world’s biggest chipmaker. The company officially parted ways with Huang on Nov. 12, after revelations about his extramarital affairs turned into a widening scandal.

Huang has admitted to a relationship with a woman that the US government reportedly believes was spying on behalf of China. Beijing has denied the espionage plot.

Nvidia’s board has formed a committee of independent directors to investigate reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the company said. The investigation will proceed to its conclusion, the company said.

See also: China’s next AI deals clouded by selloff after Anthropic IPO

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said in the statement.

Nvidia is the top maker of artificial intelligence accelerators — the chips that train and run AI models — making it the biggest beneficiary of runaway spending on data center infrastructure.

title: Tech companies are getting more creative to raise billions
article:
(Nov 23): The biggest tech companies are increasingly finding that to borrow the hundreds of billions of dollars they want to fund artificial intelligence (AI) investments, they need to get creative.

When SpaceX sold US$32 billion of bonds last week to help fund its acquisition of chips as part of a bigger financing, it didn’t sell standard corporate bonds. It set up a special purpose vehicle (SPV) that is buying the chips and leasing them to the company. The vehicle then sells bonds that look a lot like asset backed securities, but have some characteristics of corporate bonds too.

Other companies are using similar techniques. Anthropic PBC used an intricate private credit structure to get US$35 billion of financing to access Google AI chips. Meta Platforms Inc used project financing to effectively get US$12.55 billion of funding for a data centre project in Texas.

These deals are serving an important purpose for the companies: they help them borrow billions of dollars that might otherwise be difficult or impossible to raise. Anthropic, for example, at the time of the financing was a startup that hadn’t yet gone public. SpaceX is looking to hang onto its high-grade credit ratings.

But in the process of putting together these transactions, companies are blurring the lines between different debt markets, forcing high-grade corporate bond investors to look at project financings, asset backed securities, and other kinds of structured deals the money managers may never otherwise consider.

So far Wall Street is showing ample appetite for the debt, even amid growing fears of an AI bubble: bankers overseeing the deal expanded the size of the SpaceX offering to meet strong investor demand. However, investors sought higher compensation for the added complexity, securing a yield of 8.259% on a US$25.2 billion portion of bonds it sold on Thursday, a level that looks more like a junk bond.

See also: SpaceX sold US$32 bil of AI chip debt at yields topping 8% — Bloomberg

Borrowing this way allows the tech firms to get high-grade ratings on their financings — the US$25.2 billion SpaceX-vehicle bond, for example, was rated in the A tier. That in turn allows them to tap one of the deepest sources of capital for companies globally: the US$8.5 trillion US investment-grade corporate bond market.

“The pool of money in the corporate market is just much bigger,” said Himesh Lad, director of structured credit at Corbin Capital Partners. “The AI financing needs are just so large that it needs to hit all parts of the market, and you begin with the deepest ones.”

Features such as SPVs can add to complexity and can make deals more expensive. Investors need to take more time to understand the structures: figuring out how the cash flows work, what can go wrong, and which firm is on the hook for which exposure.

See also: Investors warn bond rout not over after week of soaring yields

“It’s so new,” said Davis Hebert, an analyst covering technology, media and telecom at CreditSights. “We’ve been taking a lot of client questions that are asking how strong is the lease? And there are just questions that arise around a new type of security.”

The firms getting these financings often don’t mind paying more, because their potential returns from data centers are so high that a percentage point or two of extra interest might not be material. But if the projects prove to be less profitable than hoped, every percentage point will matter.

SpaceX’s deal has a number of features more often seen in asset-backed securities. For instance, deal documents designate some of the bondholders in the deal as the “controlling class” — a feature much more commonly seen in asset-backed finance than corporate debt. And its use of an SPV means bond buyers rely heavily on the lease payments and on collateral for determining credit risk.

At the same time, some key features of the debt may mean its economic exposure is more similar to corporate deals. It is built around a “hell or high water” lease that requires SpaceX to keep making payments regardless of whether the GPUs are in use. That means the deal also depends on SpaceX’s credit risk, making the exposure in some ways more like a corporate bond.

The use of such a structure may have made the deal more difficult to swallow, at least for some.

“This is challenging for maybe some of the more traditional credit or bond traders or analysts,” Ayako Yoshioka, senior investment strategist at Wealth Enhancement Group. “The bond math is still bond math, and so I do think that that part hasn’t changed. I think the structures and the complexity is definitely the new part.”

title: CrowdStrike reaches US$44 bil cyber deal to acquire Zscaler
article:
(Nov 23): CrowdStrike Holdings Inc has agreed to acquire cybersecurity provider Zscaler Inc in one of the largest-ever deals in the sector.

The all-stock transaction values Zscaler at about US$43.9 billion, according to a statement Monday that confirmed an earlier Bloomberg News report.

Zscaler investors will receive 1.135 shares of CrowdStrike common stock for each share of Zscaler common stock they own. That represents an implied value of about US$260.41 per Zscaler share, based on CrowdStrike’s closing price on Nov 20. It’s a roughly 34% premium to Zscaler’s closing price of US$194.82 on the same day. Zscaler has a market value of around US$31.8 billion.

The deal underscores the shift towards a smaller number of companies protecting more of the world’s computers and networks. Growing fears of artificial intelligence-powered (AI) cyberattacks and security concerns around increasingly autonomous agentic AI systems have sent the valuations of cyber companies booming, helping to accelerate consolidation in the sector.

The surge in deal activity includes Alphabet Inc’s Google striking a US$32 billion takeover of Wiz, as well as ServiceNow Inc’s US$7.75 billion deal for cyber startup Armis. Palo Alto Networks Inc completed its roughly US$25 billion takeover of CyberArk in February and last week agreed to buy the AI model platform Applied Compute in an all stock deal valued at US$4.5 billion.

See also: ABB buys German cooling firm Ziehl-Abegg for US$2.2 bil

With its core Falcon product, Austin, Texas-based CrowdStrike is a leading maker of software that protects personal computers and servers. The company has a market capitalisation of almost US$235 billion. Its shares have soared alongside those of other major providers, including Palo Alto Networks and Cloudflare Inc, in lockstep with demand for cybersecurity products.

Acquiring Santa Clara, California-based Zscaler, which makes software that helps businesses protect against online threats, will give CrowdStrike a much broader role in defending corporate networks. Zscaler’s cloud-based products replace traditional virtual private networks, or VPNs, that employees use to remotely access their employers’ systems.

Legacy VPN products from companies including Citrix and Ivanti Inc have been repeatedly targeted by suspected Chinese and other state-sponsored hackers, Bloomberg has reported. Zscaler’s software gives companies greater control over who can access their networks and applications, reducing the risk that an intruder who gains access to one system can move freely through others.

See also: Japanese restaurant chain Skylark eyes more M&A after ramen chain deal

“Security used to be about keeping the adversary out. Today, safety is required to let AI in,” George Kurtz, chief executive officer and founder of CrowdStrike, said in Monday’s statement. “With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely.”

CrowdStrike’s deal for Zscaler comes on the heels of tech outages in the US this month affecting Microsoft Corp, JPMorgan Chase & Co, United Airlines and even the National Security Agency, as well as the grounding of flights in the US. Even though those incidents have been blamed on equipment and system failures, they have nevertheless elevated fears of what might happen in a cyber attacks by rogue actors.

Market researcher Gartner Inc projects that global spending on information security will grow nearly 12% this year to US$244 billion.

Qatalyst Partners is lead financial adviser to CrowdStrike, which is also working with JPMorgan Chase & Co and Bank of America Corp. BDT & MSD Partners is lead financial adviser to Zscaler, with support from Citigroup Inc and Goldman Sachs Group Inc.
